content: Patients may experience delays in receiving or returning for test results, face challenges in accessing appropriate treatment, and encounter unnecessary medical interventions such as Cesarean deliveries or the unwarranted avoidance of breastfeeding. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) concluded that the potential or identified harms associated with screening do not outweigh its benefits. The literature reviews conducted are subject to at least three significant limitations. First, there is heterogeneity in the results of individual studies, which may not be directly comparable across studies. For instance, in the context of anti-HCV positivity, some studies reported the proportion of individuals testing positive out of those tested, while others used the total population as the denominator. Additionally, there were variations in the types of healthcare providers considered for linkage-to-care and differing definitions of what constitutes treated. Second, the limitations inherent in the included studies may influence the findings of the systematic review. For example, recall bias and low response rates in individual studies could contribute to similar biases in the overall results of the systematic review. Furthermore, studies conducted in high-burden areas may not be representative of the general population, potentially affecting the external validity of the review. Finally, publication bias may skew the results, as studies reporting higher disease prevalence are more likely to be published, which could also impact the external validity of the findings. Cost-Effectiveness Considerations Recent economic analyses have provided insights into the cost-effectiveness of hepatitis C screening. For example, one analysis reported a 29% screening rate among birth cohort members and non-birth cohort members, respectively. Another analysis calculated an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of $28,000 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained when adopting a strategy of screening all individuals aged ≥18 years compared to birth cohort screening. This approach was associated with an additional 280,000 cures and 4,400 fewer cases of hepatocellular carcinoma. However, when the cure rate was reduced to 84%, the ICER increased to $39,400.
